experiments.title: What reading adds
experiments.question: The runs above assume that almost every message is read without a person, because the simulated people write in wording the offline reader knows. Real reading is not that good yet. With the two AI readers, 11% of the example messages and 27% of the unseen messages went to a person: a statement that only one reader found, or a passage neither could place. A hearing brings about 4.6 incoming messages, so this is what that adds in the typical world. With the measured shares a hearing costs 6.1 to 14.9 person-minutes, not 5.6: 60% to 84% less than by hand (37.5).

experiments.note: This table is arithmetic on two measurements, not a simulation: it does not model the delay while a reading waits for a person. Both labelled sets were written to show difficult situations, so real traffic, which is mostly routine confirmations, should sit below them. That share is the first number a pilot has to measure, and bringing it down is where the next gain is: it matters more than making anything else automatic.

findings: From 100 to 3,200 hearings (32 times more), a person's time per hearing stays between 5.6 and 5.8 minutes with the tower. By hand it is 35.5 to 38.0 minutes. People are added in proportion to exceptions, not to messages.

From 5 to 160 counties with the same 800 hearings, it goes from 5.5 to 7.1 minutes (lowest 5.4, highest 7.1). A new county is a data file (how to name the representative, deadlines, office hours), not new code. The increase is phone calls: one in five generated counties uses a "send the form, then call the clerk" process that none of the ten example counties has, and calls to an office go from 0.00 to 0.14 per hearing. Work does not grow with the number of counties. It grows with the share of counties whose own process needs a person.

Noise is what costs people time: 1.8 minutes per hearing in the quietest world, 14.6 in the roughest (by hand: 23.6 and 57.8). In the roughest world 68% of the remaining person time is phone calls and decisions after someone stayed silent. That is the next thing to attack: fewer silent counterparties, not more reading.

Letting the one-click classes go out by themselves, after a pilot has shown they are right, takes the typical world from 2.49 to 0.40 things a person does per hearing and from 5.6 to 3.9 minutes. The engine is the same; only a setting per county and class changes.

Rules checked on every step of every run (45,300 simulated hearings in 51 runs): 7 safety rules, such as "never shown ready without the authority's evidence" and "never an automatic message to a homeowner". Broken: 0. Outcome faults, such as a consultant held for two hearings at once or still held after reporting sick: 0.

Typical world: 94.2% of hearings were held with all five gates closed and 99.6% with a committed consultant. The 137 that were not fully ready were shown as open before they started, waiting on: the office: no answer yet (71%), a consultant: no answer yet (13%), a person: finding a consultant by phone (7%), a person: a phone call that is due (6%). The tower cannot make an office answer; it makes sure nobody learns that at the hearing.

Rough world: 74.3% of hearings were held with all five gates closed and 96.4% with a committed consultant. The 596 that were not fully ready were shown as open before they started, waiting on: the office: no answer yet (61%), a consultant: no answer yet (19%), a person: finding a consultant by phone (13%), a person: a phone call that is due (6%). The tower cannot make an office answer; it makes sure nobody learns that at the hearing.

"Ready" was audited against what was true in the simulated world (the consultant really can attend, the office really has the name and the file): shown ready and audited ready agree in 17 of 17 settings.
limits: The minutes are estimates, shown with a low and a high set. The comparison between sizes does not depend on them; the absolute saving does.
How often surprises happen is an assumption (the four worlds). The firm's own rates are the first thing a pilot would measure.
By hand is a favourable baseline: a person who reads every message, writes every message and makes no mistakes. Real manual work also has errors and rework, which are not counted.

The firm is cut into regional pods (counties that share consultants), about 30 hearings a week each, and each pod runs on its own. That is also how the real system would be cut, but nothing here tests one very large pod.
Reading is outside these runs: the simulated people write in wording the offline reader is known to read. What measured reading adds is in the table "What reading adds".
